issues.legal_issue: A purchaser who fails to pay the balance of the sale price within the period expressly agreed in a sale contract has not performed the contract as agreed, making a decree of specific performance on that basis erroneous.
material_facts: The sale agreement required the purchaser to pay the balance consideration within nine months.
The purchaser did not pay the balance within that period and issued a demand for a sale deed only after the period had expired.
The purchaser argued that payment depended on the sellers first measuring the property, but the Court rejected that argument.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser had not adhered to the agreed payment period, and the lower courts’ decision granting specific performance was contrary to the agreement and the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the agreed payment period was relevant to the purchaser’s performance and that the clause fell within the first part of Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963. It considered Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, but applied the principle that whether time is of the essence depends on construction of the contract as a whole. It relied on Gomathinayagam Pillai v. Palaniswami Nadar, Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, and Hind Construction Contractors v. State of Maharashtra; the latter authorities explain that contractual provisions may affect whether a time stipulation is fundamental.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract for the sale of property.
predicates.fixed_payment_deadline: The sale contract set a time by which the buyer had to pay the balance of the sale price.
predicates.buyer_missed_deadline: The buyer did not pay the balance of the sale price within the time set by the contract.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance suit concerns a sale contract with a fixed payment deadline that the buyer missed, the claim is rejected for nonperformance.

issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must plead readiness and willingness in the manner required for that remedy.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s pleading stated that he was ready and willing to pay the balance and take the sale deed.
The pleading did not conform to the prescribed allegation that the plaintiff had been and continued to be ready and willing specifically to perform the agreement after the defendant had notice of it.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff did not satisfy the mandatory pleading requirement, and the finding granting specific performance was erroneous in law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act requires the plaintiff to aver and prove performance, or continuous readiness and willingness to perform, the essential terms of the contract. Order VI Rule 3 and Form 47 in Appendix A of the Code of Civil Procedure prescribe the relevant form of pleading. The Court relied on Jugraj Singh v. Labh Singh, Ram Awadh v. Achhaibar Dubey, Ouseph Varghese v. Joseph Aley, Abdul Khader Rowther v. P.K. Sara Bai, Pushparani S. Sundaram v. Pauline Manomani James, and Manju Nath Anandappa v. Tammanasa.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract for the sale of property.
predicates.pleading_lacks_required_readiness_allega: The plaintiff’s pleading did not make the required allegation of having been and continuing to be ready and willing specifically to perform the agreement.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff seeks specific performance but the pleading lacks the required readiness-and-willingness allegation, the claim is rejected for defective pleading.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee who purchases property for value in good faith and without notice of an earlier contract is protected from specific performance of that contract against the transferee.
material_facts: The transferees obtained an encumbrance certificate and made inquiries before agreeing to purchase part of the property.
The earlier sale agreement was unregistered and was not disclosed by the encumbrance certificate.
The transferees entered into a subsequent sale agreement, obtained a registered sale deed, and paid consideration for the property.
The Court found that the transferees purchased for value in good faith and without notice of the earlier contract.
issues.conclusion: The transferees were protected as bona fide purchasers, and specific performance of the earlier contract could not be enforced against them.
issues.legal_principle: Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act protects a transferee for value who has paid the money in good faith and without notice of the original contract. The Court relied on that provision and found its requirements satisfied on the evidence.

predicates.specific_performance_claim_against_trans: A plaintiff sought specific performance of an earlier property contract against a person who later acquired the property.
predicates.transferee_acquired_for_value: The later transferee acquired the property in exchange for value and paid consideration.
predicates.transferee_acted_in_good_faith_without_n: The later transferee acted in good faith and had no notice of the earlier contract when acquiring the property.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance claim is made against a later transferee who acquired the property for value in good faith and without notice, the transferee is protected from specific performance.
